questiontext.text:
Here again is the conjecture from the worked example, and its disproof.

Conjecture: for all real numbers \(a\) and \(b\), \(a^3+b^3=(a+b)^3\).

Disproof: When \(a=4\) and \(b=1\), \(a^3+b^3=4^3+1^3=64+1=65\) and \((a+b)^3=(4+1)^3=5^3=125\). Since \(65\neq 125\), this counterexample shows that the conjecture is false.

Which sentence best summarises how this solution disproves the conjecture?

[[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]]

generalfeedback.text:
A summary of a proof names the idea that makes it work, rather than repeating the calculation. The conjecture claims that \(a^3+b^3=(a+b)^3\) for every pair of real numbers. So a single pair for which the two sides differ is enough to disprove it: that pair is a counterexample.

The best summary is therefore: It finds one pair of values for which the two sides differ, so the equation is not true for all \(a\) and \(b\).

  • It substitutes \(a=4\) and \(b=1\), and works out that \(a^3+b^3=65\) and \((a+b)^3=125\) is true, but it only describes the calculation. It does not say why the calculation disproves the conjecture.

  • It shows that \(a^3+b^3\) and \((a+b)^3\) are never equal is false. The solution checks one pair only, and in fact the two sides are equal when \(a=0\) (both are \(b^3\)).

  • It tries several pairs of values misdescribes the solution, which uses one pair. One pair is all a disproof needs.

questionvariables.text: opts1: [[sdetail, false, "It substitutes \\(a=4\\) and \\(b=1\\), and works out that \\(a^3+b^3=65\\) and \\((a+b)^3=125\\)."], [snever, false, "It shows that \\(a^3+b^3\\) and \\((a+b)^3\\) are never equal, whatever the values of \\(a\\) and \\(b\\)."], [sok, true, "It finds one pair of values for which the two sides differ, so the equation is not true for all \\(a\\) and \\(b\\)."], [smost, false, "It tries several pairs of values and finds that the two sides differ for most of them."]];

questionnote.text: Fixed: summary of the disproof of a^3+b^3=(a+b)^3 (a=4, b=1).

questiondescription.text: This question is based on Example 3.1 in Section 3 (p. 7) of Bokhove, C., Thoma, A., Gammack, D., Yu, L. H. S., Roberts, S. and Downey, F., Thinking about Proof, 1st edition, University of Southampton, 2022.

truefeedback.text: Yes. The conjecture claims the equation for every pair, so one pair where it fails is enough.

That is an accurate description of the calculation, but it does not say why the calculation disproves the conjecture. A summary names the idea that makes the argument work. What does the conjecture claim, and what does this one calculation do to that claim?

The solution checks only one pair, so it cannot tell us about every pair. In fact the two sides are equal when \(a=0\): both are \(b^3\). What is the least that a disproof of a for all statement has to show?

falsefeedback.text: This misdescribes the solution: count the pairs of values it uses. Then think about what the conjecture claims, and how many failures it takes to contradict a claim about every pair.

qtest.description: Diagnostic: accurate description, not a summary
